opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've spent a lot of time on, and my view has gotten more nuanced over the past couple of years.

The appeal of sparse autoencoders is real. You take a model's internal activations, which are dense and hard to read, and you learn a much larger dictionary of features where only a few are active at a time. Many of those features look interpretable: one fires on legal text, another on Python code, another on some specific concept. As an exploratory tool, that's genuinely useful. It gives you a vocabulary for what's happening inside the model without having to decide in advance what you're looking for.

Where I've become more skeptical is the jump from "this gives us interpretable-looking features" to "this is the right tool for controlling the model." When you actually benchmark it, for example detecting whether a concept is present, or steering the model toward or away from a behavior, SAEs often don't beat much simpler baselines. Prompting is a surprisingly strong baseline for steering. For detection, a simple linear probe or a difference-in-means direction trained on a bit of labeled data often does as well or better. And methods that learn a small intervention directly for the steering objective tend to outperform picking an SAE feature off the shelf.

Part of the reason is that SAEs are trained with an unsupervised objective: reconstruct the activations sparsely. That objective isn't the same as "find the variable I care about, in the form that's causally useful for intervening." So the concept you want might be split across several features, merged with something else, or just not cleanly there. You also pay a cost in reconstruction error, and that unexplained residual can matter a lot.

So I think of SAEs as a hypothesis-generation tool rather than a control tool. They're great for exploring and surfacing things you didn't know to look for. But once you have a concrete question, like "can I detect or steer this behavior," you should compare against strong, simple baselines and be honest about the results. The field has sometimes been too quick to treat interpretability methods as successful because the outputs look nice, rather than because they win on downstream tasks.

For me, the broader lesson is about evaluation. If interpretability is going to matter for safety and control, we need benchmarks where methods compete on things we actually care about. SAEs might earn a place there, but they have to earn it.

r001.rationale: The response says SAEs map dense internal activations into a larger dictionary of features, many of which appear interpretable and correspond to concepts or domains.

r002.rationale: The response discusses steering away from behaviors, but does not say that zeroing a coordinate representing an undesirable behavior could suppress it.

r003.rationale: The response notes that a desired concept may be split across features, merged with something else, or not cleanly represented.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about sparse autoencoders is that they're really an attempt to solve a decomposition problem. When you look at the residual stream of a transformer, you've got these dense vectors where every dimension is doing a little bit of everything, and that's not a very human-interpretable object. The hope with an SAE is that if you train a wide, sparse dictionary on those activations, the features you recover will correspond to something closer to the concepts the model is actually computing with. Things like "this token is part of a Python function name" or "the speaker is being sarcastic."

And I think the honest answer is that they've been genuinely useful as a discovery tool and somewhat disappointing as a control tool. On the discovery side, you can look at a few thousand features and find structure you wouldn't have guessed at, and that's real. It gives you a kind of browsable map of what the model represents, which is something we didn't really have before.

But when you move to steering, so actually intervening on the model, the picture gets murkier. A lot of the work I've been involved in has been comparing SAE-based steering against much simpler baselines. If you just take a difference-of-means vector between two conditions, or train a tiny supervised probe, and add that to the residual stream, you often get steering that's as good or better than clamping an SAE feature. And the baselines are cheaper and you know exactly what they're optimized for. So that raises the question of what the SAE is buying you for control specifically.

Part of the issue is that SAEs are trained on a reconstruction objective, not on a "find the causally relevant directions" objective. Sparsity is a proxy for interpretability, and it's a decent proxy, but there's no guarantee that the direction the model actually uses to implement a behavior is going to be a single dictionary element. It might be spread across several features, or it might be a direction the SAE just doesn't carve out at all because it's not the most efficient way to reconstruct activations.

So where I've landed is that if your goal is understanding, SAEs are one of the better tools we have, with the caveat that you should verify features causally and not just trust the max-activating examples. And if your goal is control, you should be asking what the task is and whether a simpler, more targeted method gets you there. I think the field is moving toward methods that bake in some notion of the task or the intervention you care about, rather than hoping unsupervised decomposition will hand you the right lever for free.

r001.rationale: The response describes training a sparse dictionary on dense activations to recover features closer to concepts the model computes with, framing SAEs as a decomposition into more interpretable representations.

r002.rationale: It discusses steering by adding vectors or clamping SAE features, but does not say that zeroing a coordinate for an undesirable behavior could suppress that behavior.

r003.rationale: The response says sparsity is only a proxy for interpretability and that a behavior’s direction may span several features or not be represented by an SAE feature, qualifying the ideal of individually interpretable features.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate understanding from control. A sparse autoencoder takes a model’s internal activations and tries to express them as a combination of relatively few features. The hope is that those features are easier to interpret than the original neurons, because a single neuron can participate in many different computations.

That gives you a useful way to explore what the model represents. You might find a feature that activates on examples with a common theme. But naming that feature isn’t the same as explaining the model. The label can miss something, and the autoencoder itself is only an approximation of the original activations.

For control, you can intervene on those features—turn one up or down—and see how the model’s output changes. That’s a stronger test than just observing what activates. But even if an intervention changes behavior, it doesn’t mean you’ve found a clean, reliable switch. It might work on one set of prompts and have unintended effects elsewhere.

So I’d treat sparse autoencoders as tools for generating and testing hypotheses. They can give us useful handles on a model’s behavior, but we still need to check what those handles actually do, how consistently they work, and what else changes when we use them.

r001.rationale: It says the autoencoder represents internal activations using relatively few features that are hoped to be easier to interpret than neurons, conveying the goal of an interpretable feature representation.

r002.rationale: It discusses turning features up or down and observing output changes, but does not say that zeroing a coordinate for undesirable behavior could suppress that behavior.

r003.rationale: It cautions that naming a feature is not the same as explaining the model and that the label can miss something, communicating that learned features are not perfectly semantically clean.

sol-6.1.text:
I think sparse autoencoders are useful as a way of generating hypotheses about what a model is doing. A model’s activations are these very high-dimensional vectors, and the hope is that you can decompose them into a larger set of features, only a few of which are active at any particular moment. Some of those features turn out to correspond to concepts or patterns that we can recognize.

But there are two separate questions: can I give a feature a compelling interpretation, and does that feature actually explain the behavior I care about? Seeing a feature activate on examples of deception doesn’t establish that you’ve found a mechanism for deception. It might be tracking the topic, or something correlated with it. You need interventions: change the feature’s activation, see what happens, and test whether that explanation holds across different contexts.

For control, that gives you a potentially useful handle. You can amplify or suppress features and sometimes change the model’s behavior. The challenge is specificity. Does suppressing an undesirable behavior also damage useful capabilities? Does the intervention work outside the examples you used to discover it? And how much relevant information is the autoencoder failing to capture?

So I’m excited about them as an experimental tool. They make it easier to formulate and test claims about internal computation. I’d be much more cautious about treating an interpretable feature as a reliable control knob, or treating a collection of those features as a complete account of the model.

r001.rationale: The response says sparse autoencoders decompose high-dimensional activations into features, some of which correspond to recognizable concepts or patterns.

r002.rationale: It describes suppressing features as a way to change behavior and specifically considers suppressing an undesirable behavior.

r003.rationale: It cautions that an apparently meaningful feature may only track a correlated topic rather than the behavior’s mechanism, showing that learned features are not always semantically clean.
